claim: A familiar good solution blocks search for a better one, even in experts (Einstellung); eye tracking shows attention stays on the familiar move.
note: Bilalic 2008 and Sheridan 2013 are independent labs, both chess. Bilalic seen by snippet only. Domain is chess; transfer to open LLM tasks is by analogy.

claim: Einstellung has a boundary: when the familiar move is a clear blunder, nearly everyone avoids it; a failure signal, not a schedule, drives the switch.
note: One study (Sheridan 2013) cited three times. Supports always-doubt only when doubt is triggered by a visible failure cue.

claim: Expertise did not protect against Einstellung when the familiar move was good but suboptimal (8/17 experts and 8/17 novices chose it).
note: Single study, n=34. c-24 reports experts resisting set rigidity in management and grammar tasks, but that source is unattributed and credibility 0; do not use.

claim: Luchins water-jar: a practiced long method persists on a later problem with a simple solution.
note: Classic result known from snippet only; open it before relying on it.

claim: Deliberate practice explains a modest share of skill differences: about 18% overall, 26% games, 21% music, 18% sports, 4% education, under 1% professions; far less than the original claim.
note: Independent: Macnamara 2014 (counted once), Macnamara 2016 sport, Macnamara and Maitra 2019 violin replication, Platz 2014 (larger for music). Same lead author on three, so independence is partial.

claim: How large the deliberate practice effect is depends on how practice is defined and on statistical reading (music rc=0.61, about a third of variance vs 36%).
note: Contested between Ericsson camp and Macnamara/Hambrick camp. Agreement only on direction: practice matters, but not all.

claim: Chess skill rests on large stores of chunks and templates; masters recall real positions far better than novices but not random ones.
note: Chase and Simon 1973 and Gobet and Simon 1996 are related lines, same research tradition; all snippet level. Template theory shows experts do better on random positions given time, so the original claim is softened.

claim: Experts sort problems by deep principle, novices by surface features.
note: Chi 1981, snippet only, small n (8 experts, 8 novices). Widely replicated in literature but not verified here.

claim: Experts first fixate the target region faster than novices (407 ms vs 719 ms): fast perceptual pattern skill.
note: Single eye-tracking study.

claim: Incubation has a small positive effect on problem solving, larger for divergent than for insight tasks; demanding break tasks weaken it.
note: One meta-analysis (Sio and Ormerod 2009) cited four times. Earlier studies conflicted. No check of post-2009 work.

claim: Brainstorming in real interacting groups produces fewer ideas than the same people working alone and pooled; blocking is the main cause.
note: Diehl and Stroebe 1987 plus Mullen 1991 meta-analysis (secondary summary only). Quality evidence weaker than quantity evidence.

claim: The group brainstorming penalty can be removed by electronic, non-blocking groups; a simple patch (writing while waiting) does not fix it.
note: c-23 is a search summary only (credibility 35) and appears to conflict with the older meta-analysis. Unsettled.

claim: Problem finding (exploring and reformulating before solving) predicts more original work in art students.
note: One cohort study; a-02 is a review of the same book. Snippet only, n unknown. No LLM test found (b-22).

claim: Intelligence correlates only weakly with creativity (r about .17).
note: Kim 2005 meta-analysis (snippet) plus Getzels cohort via review. Second source is weak; treated as single-source. Threshold-theory debate not covered.

claim: Creative thinking is ordinary thinking; no special divergent process is needed (Weisberg).
note: Same author, two books, so one source. It is a position, not a settled result. Our own data (forced divergence helped on open tasks) can be read as support or against.

claim: LLMs show fixation: early outputs constrain later ones and ideas converge on familiar solution spaces.
note: Mostly 2026 preprints (Carichon, Deng). b-13 is a search result only. Moderate confidence. Agrees with our own correlated-samples finding.

claim: Humans who use AI idea tools show more fixation and fewer, less varied ideas than unaided humans.
note: Wadinambiarachchi 2024 (n=60) and Holzner 2025 meta-analysis (GenAI reduces diversity in human-AI work). Abstract level.

claim: Open-ended LLM output is homogeneous within and across models.
note: Artificial Hivemind benchmark is strong (26K queries). Fits our NoveltyBench result.

claim: Chain-of-thought reduced fixation in LLMs but not in humans.
note: One preprint, abstract only.

claim: Stronger reasoning models fall into Einstellung traps less often.
note: One medical-domain preprint, abstract only. Suggests forced doubt may matter less as models improve.

claim: Persona prompts do not reliably raise LLM creativity; temperature helps novelty up to a point then coherence drops. Ordinary personas can raise diversity.
note: Huang 2025 says persona does not help; Deng 2026 says ordinary personas help diversity. Different measures (DAT vs idea partitioning).

claim: GenAI is on average not different from humans in creative performance and has not clearly surpassed them.
note: Two meta-analyses plus a large DAT study. Effects driven by a few large studies.

claim: LLM research ideas look more novel than expert ideas at ideation but lose most of that advantage after execution.
note: Same research group, two stages of one program. Strong design, but one source. Warns that novelty alone is not the goal.

claim: Revising an answer with no outside feedback does not help LLM reasoning and can hurt.
note: Huang 2023 preprint. Matches our scaffold-hurts-single-answer finding. Needs a second source.

claim: Shown examples cause designers to copy example features (design fixation).
note: Jansson and Smith from secondary pages; Wadinambiarachchi 2024 gives a direct experiment with AI examples. c-20 says the mechanism may be a used-up solution pool, not conformity.

claim: Telling designers about fixation reduces it.
note: Snippet, credibility 40. Weak.

claim: Chess masters needed very different practice hours to reach master level (3,016 to 23,608).
note: Secondary citation of Gobet and Campitelli 2007.
